recipe.history:
The tomato — Solanum lycopersicum — is native to western South America, where wild species grew along the Andes from present-day Peru to Ecuador. The Aztec civilization in Mesoamerica was among the first to cultivate and cook with the fruit, calling it tomatl in Nahuatl, and incorporating it into sauces and stews long before European contact. Spanish colonizers brought the tomato back to Europe in the sixteenth century, where it was initially regarded with deep suspicion — its membership in the nightshade family prompted fears of toxicity, and for decades it was grown as an ornamental plant rather than a food. It was in southern Italy and Spain that the tomato first shed its sinister reputation and found its culinary destiny, appearing in cooked sauces by the late 1600s. From there, the fruit spread through Mediterranean cuisine, transforming pasta, pizza, and braised dishes into the iconic forms we recognize today.

The tomato arrived in American cooking through multiple cultural channels: Italian immigrants brought their sauce traditions to the urban Northeast, Mexican and Tex-Mex cuisine kept the tomato central in salsas and guacamole bases, and Southern Appalachian canning culture enshrined it as a pantry staple. By the mid-twentieth century the thick-sliced beefsteak tomato had become the canonical burger topping across American diners and backyard grills alike — a cool, acidic counterpoint to hot, fatty beef. The Sun Gold cherry tomato, developed in Japan and introduced to American markets in the 1990s, brought a new sweetness and poppy brightness to the table. Sun-dried tomatoes, popularized in the 1980s California cuisine movement, offered concentrated umami depth. Roasted tomatoes, a technique borrowed from Spanish sofrito tradition, added caramelized sweetness. Each preparation unlocks a different facet of the same fruit, and together they compose a portrait of everything the tomato can be.

I remember the summer my neighbor Mrs. Calloway grew Sun Gold cherry tomatoes along her back fence, and she would bring over a pint every Saturday morning still warm from the vine. I was maybe nine years old and I didn't know yet that a tomato could taste like candy, like something the sun had poured itself into directly. My mother would slice a big beefsteak over a plate, fan the wedges out, salt them heavily, and let them weep their juice into the ceramic. We ate them standing at the kitchen counter. Years later, working a summer in a restaurant kitchen, I learned to slow-roast Roma tomatoes overnight with olive oil and thyme until they collapsed into something almost jammy and impossibly sweet. Those three tomato memories — the warm Sun Gold from the fence, the salted beefsteak slices, the midnight-roasted Roma — live in the same place in my mind, and this burger is my attempt to stack all three of them into one bite.

I cook every beef patty to medium rare, and I will not apologize for it. Medium rare — that internal temperature window of 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is where the Maillard-browned crust and the still-rosy, yielding interior exist in perfect tension. The fat in a properly blended patty has begun to render and lubricate every fiber without fully evacuating, so each bite is simultaneously crisp at the edges and molten at the center. Cooking beyond medium rare drives out moisture through protein contraction, tightening the muscle fibers until the patty becomes a dry, gray puck that no amount of sauce or topping can redeem. The tomato in all its forms — bright, acidic, sweet — needs a juicy, blushing patty underneath it as a counterpart, not a charred hockey puck. Medium rare is not a preference. It is the answer the meat gives when you ask it what it wants to become.
ingredients: 4 large eggs (3 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
6 tbsp unsalted butter, softened and cubed
1/2 cup sun-dried tomatoes in oil, drained
1 pint Sun Gold cherry tomatoes, halved
instructions: 1. Make the roasted tomatoes: Preheat oven to 275°F. Place halved Roma tomatoes cut-side up on a parchment-lined baking sheet. Drizzle with olive oil, sprinkle with thyme, salt, pepper, and sugar. Roast for 2 to 2.5 hours until collapsed, caramelized, and concentrated. Remove and let cool. These can be made a day ahead.

2. Make the brioche buns: Combine warm milk, warm water, and yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer. Stir and let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add sugar, salt, and 3 eggs. Add flour one cup at a time, mixing with the dough hook on low until a shaggy dough forms.

3. Increase mixer speed to medium and add softened butter one or two cubes at a time, waiting for each addition to incorporate before adding the next. Mix 8 to 10 minutes until dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls away from the bowl sides cleanly.
4. Transfer dough to a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and refrigerate overnight or for at least 8 hours for a slow, flavor-developing rise.

5. Remove dough from refrigerator. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 130g each). Shape each portion into a tight ball by pulling the surface taut and pinching the seam underneath. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, spacing 3 inches apart. Cover loosely and let proof at room temperature 1.5 to 2 hours until puffy and nearly doubled.

6. Preheat oven to 375°F. Whisk remaining egg with 1 tbsp water. Brush buns gently with egg wash and sprinkle sesame seeds on top. Bake 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden brown. Cool on a wire rack before slicing.

7. Make the sun-dried tomato aioli: Combine sun-dried tomatoes, mayonnaise, garlic, lemon juice, and smoked paprika in a blender. Blend until completely smooth. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.
8. Prepare the Sun Gold cherry tomatoes: Toss halved Sun Gold tomatoes with olive oil and a pinch of flaky sea salt. Set aside at room temperature.

9. Form the patties: Gently divide ground beef into 4 equal portions without overworking. Form into patties about 4 inches wide and 3/4-inch thick. Press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty with your thumb. Season both sides generously with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Refrigerate 15 minutes.

10. Preheat a cast-iron skillet or griddle over high heat for 3 minutes. Lightly oil the surface. Place patties dimple-side up and cook undisturbed for 3 minutes until a deep crust forms on the bottom.

11. Flip patties once. Lay a slice of fresh mozzarella on each patty. Cook 2 to 3 minutes more until internal temperature reads 130 to 135°F on an instant-read thermometer. Remove patties from heat and tent loosely with foil. Rest 3 minutes — temperature will carry over to 133 to 137°F.
12. While patties rest, split buns and toast cut-side down in butter in the same skillet over medium heat until golden, about 90 seconds.

13. Assemble the burgers: Spread a generous layer of sun-dried tomato aioli on both cut sides of the bun. On the bottom bun, layer two thick slices of beefsteak tomato. Place the rested patty with melted mozzarella on top. Add two or three roasted Roma tomato halves. Spoon a pile of Sun Gold cherry tomatoes over the top. Tuck in several fresh basil leaves. Drizzle with balsamic glaze. Close with the top bun. Serve immediately.
